enonce_markdown: In the wiring of a house, a fuse is fitted to protect an appliance. In which wire should the fuse be connected?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A fuse is a safety device that melts when the current is too large. It must be placed in the live wire so that, when it melts, the appliance is cut off from the high-voltage supply.

### Solution

With the fuse in the **live wire**, a fault current melts the fuse and the appliance is disconnected from the live (high-voltage) side. If the fuse were in the neutral wire, the appliance would stay connected to the live wire after the fuse blew and could still give a shock. The earth wire carries current only in a fault and must never be broken.

The correct option is **a**.

choix.texte: Any one of the three wires, because the same current flows in all of them

enonce_markdown: Two lamps in a living room are connected in parallel to the mains supply. The filament of one lamp breaks. What happens to the other lamp?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In a parallel circuit each branch is connected directly across the supply, so each branch has the full supply voltage and works independently of the others.

### Solution

Each lamp has its own path across the mains voltage. When one filament breaks, only that branch is broken; the other lamp still has the full mains voltage across it, so it **stays lit at the same brightness**. This is why houses are wired in parallel.

- Option a describes a series circuit.
- Options b and d suggest the voltage across the lamp would change, which does not happen in a parallel connection.

The correct option is **c**.

choix.texte: It goes out, because the circuit is broken
It becomes dimmer, because the current has one path less
It stays lit at the same brightness
It becomes brighter, because it now receives all the current

enonce_markdown: An electric blender in a Douala kitchen is rated $450\,\mathrm{W}$, $220\,\mathrm{V}$. The plug can be fitted with a $1\,\mathrm{A}$, $3\,\mathrm{A}$, $5\,\mathrm{A}$ or $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse. Which is the lowest-rated fuse that will not blow when the blender is working normally?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Use $P = IV$ to find the normal working current, $I = \dfrac{P}{V}$. The fuse rating must be just above this current, so the fuse does not blow in normal use but still protects the appliance if the current rises.

### Solution

$I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{450\,\mathrm{W}}{220\,\mathrm{V}} = 2.05\,\mathrm{A}$.

The fuse rating must be greater than $2.05\,\mathrm{A}$. The $1\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would blow at once. The lowest rating above $2.05\,\mathrm{A}$ is **$3\,\mathrm{A}$**. Larger fuses ($5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$) would also let the blender work, but they would allow a much larger fault current before melting, so they protect the blender less well.

The correct option is **b**.

enonce_markdown: A shopkeeper in Limbe uses four $40\,\mathrm{W}$ lamps for $5$ hours every day. The electricity company charges $60$ FCFA per kWh. What is the cost of running the four lamps for $30$ days?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Energy in kWh $=$ power in kW $\times$ time in hours. Cost $=$ energy in kWh $\times$ price per kWh. Convert watts to kilowatts by dividing by $1000$, and count all appliances and all days.

### Solution

Total power $= 4\times 40 = 160\,\mathrm{W} = 0.16\,\mathrm{kW}$.

Energy $= 0.16\,\mathrm{kW}\times 5\,\mathrm{h}\times 30 = 24\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

Cost $= 24\times 60 = 1440$ FCFA.

- $12$ FCFA is one lamp for one day.
- $48$ FCFA is four lamps for one day (the $30$ days are forgotten).
- $360$ FCFA is one lamp for $30$ days (the number of lamps is forgotten).

The correct option is **d**.

enonce_markdown:
A family plugs an electric iron ($1200\,\mathrm{W}$), an electric kettle ($900\,\mathrm{W}$) and a room heater ($1000\,\mathrm{W}$) into one extension socket in their house. The mains voltage is $220\,\mathrm{V}$ and the plug of the extension lead contains a $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse. All three appliances are switched on together.

(a) Calculate the total power drawn from the socket.

(b) Calculate the total current in the lead.

(c) State, with a reason, what happens to the fuse.

(d) A student suggests replacing the $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse with a piece of thick copper wire. Explain why this is dangerous.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Appliances on one socket are in parallel, so their powers add and so do their currents. Use $P = IV$, so $I = \dfrac{P}{V}$, and compare the current with the rating of the fuse.

### Solution

(a) Total power $= 1200 + 900 + 1000 = 3100\,\mathrm{W}$.

(b) $I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{3100\,\mathrm{W}}{220\,\mathrm{V}} = 14.1\,\mathrm{A}$.

(c) The current of $14.1\,\mathrm{A}$ is greater than the fuse rating of $13\,\mathrm{A}$ (a $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse only allows $13\times 220 = 2860\,\mathrm{W}$), so the fuse wire **overheats, melts and breaks the circuit**, switching all three appliances off.

(d) A thick copper wire would never melt, so the lead would carry too large a current without any warning. The cable of the lead would overheat, its insulation would melt, and this could cause a **fire** or a short circuit. The fuse must have a rating just above the normal current so that it melts before the wiring is damaged.

enonce_markdown:
In a house in Buea, a refrigerator ($150\,\mathrm{W}$) runs for $12$ hours a day, four lamps of $25\,\mathrm{W}$ each are on for $6$ hours a day, and a television ($80\,\mathrm{W}$) is on for $5$ hours a day. Electricity costs $75$ FCFA per kWh.

(a) Calculate the electrical energy used each day by (i) the refrigerator, (ii) the four lamps, (iii) the television, all in kWh.

(b) Calculate the total energy used in a month of $30$ days, and the cost.

(c) The family buys prepaid credit worth $10\,000$ FCFA. Calculate the number of kWh bought, and for how many complete days it lasts at this rate of use.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Electrical energy (kWh) $=$ power (kW) $\times$ time (h). Add the daily energies, multiply by the number of days, and then by the price per kWh. For prepaid credit, divide the money by the price to get the energy bought, then divide by the daily energy.

### Solution

(a) (i) Refrigerator: $0.150\,\mathrm{kW}\times 12\,\mathrm{h} = 1.8\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

(ii) Lamps: total power $= 4\times 25 = 100\,\mathrm{W} = 0.100\,\mathrm{kW}$, so energy $= 0.100\times 6 = 0.6\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

(iii) Television: $0.080\,\mathrm{kW}\times 5\,\mathrm{h} = 0.4\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

(b) Daily total $= 1.8 + 0.6 + 0.4 = 2.8\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

Month: $2.8\times 30 = 84\,\mathrm{kWh}$. Cost $= 84\times 75 = 6300$ FCFA.

(c) Energy bought $= \dfrac{10\,000}{75} = 133.3\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

Number of days $= \dfrac{133.3}{2.8} = 47.6$, so the credit lasts **47 complete days**.
